title: Entanglement without distillable secret key
formal: Do there exist finite integers \(a,b\ge2\) and an entangled density matrix \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^a\otimes\mathbb C^b\) with zero distillable secret-key rate, \(K_D(\rho)=0\), under arbitrary local quantum operations and two-way public classical communication? The rate is the standard asymptotic, vanishing-error rate defined below. There is no restriction to one-way communication, perfect finite-block output, a chosen measurement, or efficient protocols.

source_formulation.text: So far, it is known that separable, i.e., disentangled states, are useless [43], while it remains open if entangled but key-undistillable states exist.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 3

why: This question determines whether every entangled bipartite state has some usable private correlation when arbitrary collective quantum processing is allowed. An entangled zero-key state would establish an additional form of irreversibility beyond ordinary bound entanglement; a universal positivity theorem would identify entanglement itself as the exact boundary for asymptotic key usefulness.
status_note: Source-open. On 16 September 2026 the full official May 2026 source and March one-way no-go paper, primary historical key abstract, July classical bound-information abstract and bounded later-work searches were checked. The source explicitly assumes the negative answer rather than proving it. One-way exact key obstructions and classical bound information do not establish an entangled zero-key state under the retained two-way vanishing-error model. No verified resolution was found; cited proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.

progress.text: Private-state methods demonstrate secret key from some states with no distillable entanglement.
A no-go theorem for heralded exact one-way key is published; its restrictions differ from the asymptotic two-way target.
The source explicitly retains the existence of entangled key-undistillable states as an open question and builds its cost theory under their nonexistence assumption.
A classical bound-information construction is posted; its classical source model does not settle unrestricted quantum key distillation.

importance.reason: A central unresolved boundary between entanglement and private communication, directly controlling assumptions in the resource theory of quantum secret key.
importance.basis: Individual review of the May 2026 source and related primary results on 16 September 2026.

sentences: Shared quantum states can sometimes be converted into secret classical keys by local operations and public communication.
This project asks whether there are entangled states from which no secret key can be distilled.
Separable states provide a known class of useless resources, but entanglement alone does not immediately determine the distillable-key rate.
The question is also different from asking whether an entangled state can produce maximally entangled pairs.
Identifying an entangled key-undistillable state, or proving that none exists, would settle a basic boundary in the resource theory of private communication.

definitions:
A state on a finite-dimensional complex vector space is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one. Hermitian means \(X=X^\dagger\), with dagger denoting conjugate transpose; positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger Xv\ge0\) for every vector \(v\); trace is the sum of diagonal entries. The state \(\rho\) is separable if \(\rho=\sum_jp_j\sigma_j\otimes\tau_j\) for some finite list of local states \(\sigma_j,\tau_j\) and real weights \(p_j\ge0\), \(\sum_jp_j=1\). It is entangled if no such decomposition exists. All matrix entries may be arbitrary complex numbers.

A local quantum instrument has finitely many outcomes \(t\). Outcome \(t\) sends a local matrix \(X\) to \(\mathcal E_t(X)=\sum_jA_{t,j}XA_{t,j}^\dagger\), where the rectangular matrices \(A_{t,j}\) obey \(\sum_{t,j}A_{t,j}^\dagger A_{t,j}=I\). On a normalized input, \(\operatorname{Tr}\mathcal E_t(X)\) is the outcome probability and division by this probability gives the conditional state. An LOCC protocol is a finite adaptive sequence of these instruments performed alternately in the two laboratories. An outcome may be sent as a classical message to the other party; later instruments may depend on the messages and local outcomes already available. Classical communication is public and can proceed in both directions. Local ancillary states, local randomness, public shared randomness and discarding local systems are allowed. No extra shared entangled state, preshared secret key or quantum communication is supplied. The resulting map \(\Lambda\), including all outcomes rather than conditioning for free on a success branch, is trace preserving. Each protocol may have arbitrarily many finite rounds and finite-dimensional ancillary systems; their sizes may grow with the number of input copies. There is no bound on local computation, no finite gate-set restriction and no uniformity requirement on the sequence of protocols. Finite-round approximations suffice for the vanishing-error rate, so allowing limits of LOCC maps on fixed finite systems does not change the target.

For an integer \(M\ge1\), a private state with key dimension \(M\) has the form \[\gamma=\frac1M\sum_{i,j=0}^{M-1}|i\rangle\langle j|_{K_A}\otimes|i\rangle\langle j|_{K_B}\otimes U_i\sigma U_j^\dagger.\] Here \(K_A,K_B\cong\mathbb C^M\) are the local key registers, \(\sigma\) is an arbitrary state on finite local shield systems \(S_A\otimes S_B\), and each \(U_i\) is a unitary matrix on the joint shield space. This is a mathematical description of the target state; applying these joint unitaries is not a free operation available to the two parties. The physical output partition is \((K_AS_A):(K_BS_B)\). Measuring both key registers in the displayed basis gives the same uniform symbol, independent of any purifying external system, hence \(\log_2M\) bits of secret key. The shields remain local output systems. For matrices on the same space, trace distance is \(D(X,Y)=\tfrac12\|X-Y\|_1\), where \(\|Z\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{Z^\dagger Z}\).

A real rate \(R\ge0\) is achievable from \(\rho\) if there are, for every integer \(n\ge1\), a protocol \(\Lambda_n\) acting on \(n\) independent copies \(\rho^{\otimes n}\), an integer \(M_n\ge1\), and a private state \(\gamma_n\) of key dimension \(M_n\) on the protocol's output systems, such that \[D\bigl(\Lambda_n(\rho^{\otimes n}),\gamma_n\bigr)\longrightarrow0,\qquad \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2M_n}{n}\ge R.\] The private states, shields and protocols can depend on \(n\) and \(\rho\). Define \(K_D(\rho)\) as the supremum of achievable rates. The zero rate is always available. Thus zero distillable key means no strictly positive rate with error tending to zero, not merely inability to produce one exact secret bit at a particular block size. The private-state formulation is equivalent to local quantum operations and public communication that produce classical keys secure against an eavesdropper holding a purification of the input state.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that some finite-dimensional entangled state has \(K_D=0\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that every such entangled state has \(K_D>0\). The same chosen state must defeat every allowed protocol sequence in an affirmative existence proof. Refuting existence may use a state-dependent strictly positive rate, with no rate uniform over all entangled states. Failure of one-way protocols, an exact-output no-go theorem, or zero key after one chosen local measurement is insufficient. Conversely, proving arbitrarily small positive rates for a sequence of different states does not exhibit a state of zero rate. The target is an exact yes/no assertion about positivity; an additive estimate of the rate cannot replace it.

context_blocks.text: Secret-key distillation asks two parties to turn a noisy shared quantum resource into matching random data unavailable to an eavesdropper. Entanglement is necessary, but the open issue is whether it is always sufficient for some positive asymptotic rate.

The source develops a theory of the cost of creating quantum secret key under the explicit assumption that entangled states with zero distillable key do not exist. Its conditional theorems therefore do not answer this existence question.

Bound entanglement obstructs producing maximally entangled pairs. Horodecki and coauthors nevertheless show that certain bound-entangled states yield secret key, so zero distillable entanglement cannot be substituted for zero distillable key.

The March 2026 no-go theorem concerns heralded exact key and one-way classical communication. It explicitly exhibits a gap from approximate key distillation. The present target permits vanishing error and two-way messages, so that no-go theorem is not a counterexample here.

The July 2026 classical bound-information preprint concerns three classical random variables supplied to the parties and an eavesdropper. The abstract also distinguishes particular measurements of quantum states from the original states. Such a fixed classical distribution does not rule out all collective local quantum operations on an entangled input state.
